sections.normalized_html: A circle has center [MATH: O,] and points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] lie on the circle. The measure of arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] is [MATH: 84^\circ.] What is the measure of [MATH: \angle OAB,] in degrees?
sections.readable_text: A circle has center [MATH: O,] and points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] lie on the circle. The measure of arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] is [MATH: 84^\circ.] What is the measure of [MATH: \angle OAB,] in degrees?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: \overline{OA}] and [MATH: \overline{OB}] are both radii of the circle, triangle [MATH: OAB] is isosceles with [MATH: OA = OB.] Thus, the base angles [MATH: \angle OAB] and [MATH: \angle OBA] are congruent.

In [MATH: \triangle OAB,] the measures of the interior angles sum to [MATH: 180^\circ{:}] [MATH: m\angle OAB + m\angle OBA + m\angle AOB = 180^\circ]

We are given that [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{AB} = 84^\circ.] Since [MATH: \angle AOB] is the central angle corresponding to arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB},] we have [MATH: m\angle AOB = 84^\circ.]

Now, since [MATH: m\angle OAB = m\angle OBA,] we let each equal [MATH: x.] Substituting, we solve for [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: x + x + 84^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 2x + 84^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 2x|= 96^{∘}; x|= 48^{∘}]

Therefore, the measure of [MATH: \angle OAB] is [MATH: m\angle OAB = 48^\circ.]

sections.normalized_html: Points [MATH: M] and [MATH: N] lie on a circle with center [MATH: O.] The radius of the circle is [MATH: 9\,\mathrm{cm}.] Triangle [MATH: OMN] has a perimeter of [MATH: 29 \: \text{cm}.] What is the length, in centimeters, of [MATH: MN?]
sections.readable_text: Points [MATH: M] and [MATH: N] lie on a circle with center [MATH: O.] The radius of the circle is [MATH: 9\,\mathrm{cm}.] Triangle [MATH: OMN] has a perimeter of [MATH: 29 \: \text{cm}.] What is the length, in centimeters, of [MATH: MN?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The triangle [MATH: OMN] is formed by connecting the center [MATH: O] to two points on the circle, [MATH: M] and [MATH: N.] In this triangle, the segments [MATH: \overline{OM}] and [MATH: \overline{ON}] are both radii of the circle, which means [MATH: OM = ON = 9 \: \text{cm}.]

Now, the perimeter of triangle [MATH: OMN] is given by [MATH: p = OM + ON + MN.]

Therefore, since the perimeter of [MATH: \triangle OMN] is [MATH: 29,] we can solve for MN the follwoing eqaution: [MATH: p|= OM + ON + MN; 29|= 9 + 9 + MN; 29|= 18 + MN; MN|= 29 − 18; = 11cm]

items.title: Determining Base Angles of Central Triangles Using the Distance Formula

sections.normalized_html: In the [MATH: xy]-plane, a circle has center [MATH: O] with coordinates [MATH: (a, b).] Points [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] lie on the circle. Point [MATH: P] has coordinates [MATH: (a+4, b+\sqrt{18}),] and [MATH: \angle{POQ}] is a right angle. What is the length of [MATH: \overline{PQ}?]
sections.readable_text: In the [MATH: xy]-plane, a circle has center [MATH: O] with coordinates [MATH: (a, b).] Points [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] lie on the circle. Point [MATH: P] has coordinates [MATH: (a+4, b+\sqrt{18}),] and [MATH: \angle{POQ}] is a right angle. What is the length of [MATH: \overline{PQ}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are given that [MATH: O] is the center of the circle, and [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] lie on the circle. Therefore, [MATH: \overline{OP}] and [MATH: \overline{OQ}] are radii of the circle. Hence, [MATH: OP = OQ.]

We know that the coordinates of [MATH: O] and [MATH: P] are [MATH: (a, b)] and [MATH: (a+4, b+\sqrt{18}),] respectively. Hence, we can calculate [MATH: OP] using the distance formula: [MATH: OP|= sqrt((x_{2} − x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} − y_{1})^{2}); = sqrt((a + 4 − a)^{2} + (b + sqrt(18) − b)^{2}); = sqrt(4^{2} + (sqrt(18))^{2}); = sqrt(16 + 18); = sqrt(34)] Thus, [MATH: OQ = OP = \sqrt{34}.]

Finally, [MATH: \triangle{POQ}] is a right triangle because [MATH: \angle{POQ}] is a right angle. Therefore, applying the Pythagorean theorem, we have [MATH: PQ^{2}|= OP^{2} + OQ^{2}; = OP^{2} + OP^{2}; = 2OP^{2}; = 2(sqrt(34))^{2}; = 2(34); = 68.]

Consequently, [MATH: PQ|= sqrt(68); = sqrt(4 ⋅ 17); = sqrt(4) ⋅ sqrt(17); = 2sqrt(17).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we draw a circle with center [MATH: O,] and place any two distinct points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] on the circle.
If we connect points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] to the center [MATH: O,] then we create a central angle [MATH: \angle{AOB}] and an arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b76c00eb9ad720086c51063503925190]

Content:
Notice that the central angle [MATH: \angle{AOB}] subtends the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB},] and since the measure of a central angle is equal to the measure of its intercepted arc, their measures must be equal:
[MATH: m\angle{AOB} = m\overset{\frown}{AB}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining the Central Angle Corresponding to an Arc and Vice Versa

Example Prompt:
Point [MATH: O] is the center of a circle, and points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] lie on the circumference. The measure of angle [MATH: \angle AOB] is [MATH: 82^\circ.] What is the measure, in degrees, of its associated arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/2b97023e3d6c1f117db3a02f3b858f30]

The central angle [MATH: \angle AOB] subtends arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB},] and since the measure of a central angle is equal to the measure of its intercepted arc, we have
[MATH: m \overset{\frown}{AB} = 82\,^\circ.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Isosceles Triangles in Circles

Content:
Consider again our circle with center [MATH: O] connected to any two distinct points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] on the circle.
If we also connect the points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] then we create the triangle [MATH: \triangle{OAB},] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4594b5cf53051c6bf1cd7a24ca01d613]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \overline{OA}] and [MATH: \overline{OB}] are both radii of the circle, so must have equal measures: [MATH: OA=OB.]
As a result, we immediately see that triangle [MATH: \triangle{OAB}] is isoceles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/53f3003d1817caef54e0e8e92d734150]

Content:
Furthermore, by the Isosceles Triangle Theorem, the two non-central angles are congruent: [MATH: m\angle{OAB} = m\angle{ABO}.]

Content:
This simple observation—that connecting two points on a circle to the circle’s center creates an isosceles triangle—is used frequently in circle geometry. Let's see how in the next example.

---

Item 6 — Example: Determining Base Angles of Central Triangles

Example Prompt:
A circle has center [MATH: O,] and points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] lie on the circle. The measure of arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] is [MATH: 84^\circ.] What is the measure of [MATH: \angle OAB,] in degrees?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/bbf94f3b7adef1c058062347faa74f6f]

Since [MATH: \overline{OA}] and [MATH: \overline{OB}] are both radii of the circle, triangle [MATH: OAB] is isosceles with [MATH: OA = OB.] Thus, the base angles [MATH: \angle OAB] and [MATH: \angle OBA] are congruent.

In [MATH: \triangle OAB,] the measures of the interior angles sum to [MATH: 180^\circ{:}]
[MATH: m\angle OAB + m\angle OBA + m\angle AOB = 180^\circ]

We are given that [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{AB} = 84^\circ.] Since [MATH: \angle AOB] is the central angle corresponding to arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB},] we have
[MATH: m\angle AOB = 84^\circ.]

Now, since [MATH: m\angle OAB = m\angle OBA,] we let each equal [MATH: x.] Substituting, we solve for [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: x + x + 84^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 2x + 84^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 2x|= 96^{∘}; x|= 48^{∘}]

Therefore, the measure of [MATH: \angle OAB] is
[MATH: m\angle OAB = 48^\circ.]

Item 9 — Example: Determining Base Lengths of Central Triangles

Example Prompt:
Points [MATH: M] and [MATH: N] lie on a circle with center [MATH: O.] The radius of the circle is [MATH: 9\,\mathrm{cm}.] Triangle [MATH: OMN] has a perimeter of [MATH: 29 \: \text{cm}.] What is the length, in centimeters, of [MATH: MN?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/90d4e9d08a5e307793cf26af80e1042b]

The triangle [MATH: OMN] is formed by connecting the center [MATH: O] to two points on the circle, [MATH: M] and [MATH: N.] In this triangle, the segments [MATH: \overline{OM}] and [MATH: \overline{ON}] are both radii of the circle, which means
[MATH: OM = ON = 9 \: \text{cm}.]

Now, the perimeter of triangle [MATH: OMN] is given by
[MATH: p = OM + ON + MN.]

Therefore, since the perimeter of [MATH: \triangle OMN] is [MATH: 29,] we can solve for MN the follwoing eqaution:
[MATH: p|= OM + ON + MN; 29|= 9 + 9 + MN; 29|= 18 + MN; MN|= 29 − 18; = 11cm]

EXPLANATION

[IMG: /graphics/724e343ce1b8b761729537fe99465506]

We are given that [MATH: O] is the center of the circle, and [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] lie on the circle. Therefore, [MATH: \overline{OP}] and [MATH: \overline{OQ}] are radii of the circle. Hence, [MATH: OP = OQ.]

We know that the coordinates of [MATH: O] and [MATH: P] are [MATH: (a, b)] and [MATH: (a+4, b+\sqrt{18}),] respectively. Hence, we can calculate [MATH: OP] using the distance formula:
[MATH: OP|= sqrt((x_{2} − x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} − y_{1})^{2}); = sqrt((a + 4 − a)^{2} + (b + sqrt(18) − b)^{2}); = sqrt(4^{2} + (sqrt(18))^{2}); = sqrt(16 + 18); = sqrt(34)]
Thus, [MATH: OQ = OP = \sqrt{34}.]

Finally, [MATH: \triangle{POQ}] is a right triangle because [MATH: \angle{POQ}] is a right angle. Therefore, applying the Pythagorean theorem, we have
[MATH: PQ^{2}|= OP^{2} + OQ^{2}; = OP^{2} + OP^{2}; = 2OP^{2}; = 2(sqrt(34))^{2}; = 2(34); = 68.]

Consequently,
[MATH: PQ|= sqrt(68); = sqrt(4 ⋅ 17); = sqrt(4) ⋅ sqrt(17); = 2sqrt(17).]
